utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Wednesday, 15th of July, 2009. Let me first greet Mr. Praljak. My greetings to Mr. Prlic, Mr. Stojic, Mr. Petkovic, and Mr. Pusic, without forgetting Mr. Stojic. Good afternoon, Mr. Stringer, Mr. Scott, and your associates. And I'd like to greet the staff members working with us today. First, a housekeeping announcement. We can sit tomorrow morning rather than in the afternoon. We'll sit from 9.00 to quarter to 2:00 tomorrow. Whenever we can sit in the morning, we may as well use the opportunity. It's less tiring for everybody to work in the morning. I hope you're available tomorrow morning, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we're available. Again, I express my appreciation of the Trial Chamber and the Registry for sticking to today's original schedule, which allowed me to take care of my business this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Ms. Pinter, I believe have you some corrections to make to yesterday's transcript. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. I'm talking about the record made on the 14th of July, 2009. Page 43036, line 25, instead of "HV," there should be "HVO." Page 43052, line 17, instead of "Klopopan," we should have "Klopotan." Page 43055, lines 18, 19 and 20, and also page 43056, line 13, instead of the word "request," there should be "order." Page 43084, line 25, instead of the word "both," we should have the word "boats." Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Pinter. Mr. Stringer, you may proceed to continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good afternoon to you. Good afternoon, Your Honours, Counsel, everyone else in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. Good afternoon, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm a bit farther away from you today. Maybe you'll like that better. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, yesterday afternoon or evening, when we finished our work, we had been looking at Exhibit P06037, which is in the binder there, which was the report from Mr. Boricic, who was with the trainings organ of the 5th Guards Brigade, and it was a report that he sent to Brigadier Kapular of the 5th Guards Brigade of the Croatian Army. Do you remember when we were talking about this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And we were talking about the various components of the 5th Guards Brigade and the places where they were deployed. As indicated in here and in some other documents, we were talking about Mostar, Rastani, I believe, Prozor, Gornji Vakuf, as being some of the locations, anyway, where members of the Croatian Army came and fought with the HVO. Do you remember us talking about that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember. However, members of the Croatian Army did not fight against the HVO -- or did not fight with the HVO. They were members of the HVO as volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And just going back to something you said yesterday, and I'll use this as our starting point, yesterday you said, and I'll read this verbatim from the transcript, you said: "I can confirm that some of the members of the 5th Guards Brigade, some of the volunteers, participated in the battle-field as HVO units in Mostar, Bijelo Polje, at the beginning, but mostly in Vakuf, but the figure was never more than 250 men at any given point in time." Do you recall saying that yesterday, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember, and this covers the period during which I was the Commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Right. And, in fact, that's the period that I've primarily been trying to focus on with this -- with this set of documents. General, let me take you to another document in the binder. It's closer to the front of the binder. We skipped over it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, we're going to go through the documents submitted to you by the Prosecutor. You understand that the Prosecutor is presenting these documents as part of his case; namely, that the Republic of Croatia controlled the HVO. I know that you have not read the trial judgements, you said so, but for you to be properly informed of everything let me remind you that our Trial Chamber, on the 7th of December, 2006, issued a decision on motions of the 14th and 23rd of June, 2006, for judicial notice of admitted facts. As part of the decision, the Trial Chamber decided to do judicial notice of paragraph 200 of the Naletilic judgement. Let me read it out to you slowly for you to hear it properly. This is what the Naletilic Trial Chamber wrote and what our Trial Chamber, at the beginning of the trial, established as judicial notice. I read you the entire sentence, each word being important. Quote: "Croatia participated in the organisation, planning or coordinating military operations conducted in the framework of the conflict between the HVO and the ABiH." Naletilic judgement, paragraph 200. In other words, other Trial Judges, in their judgements, had made the finding that military operations conducted by the HVO against the ABiH had been organised, planned, and coordinated by the Republic of Croatia. There it is. Keep this in mind, please. Judicial notice is part of the proceedings, but it can be challenged, depending on the evidence adduced that would go -- show the opposite. Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, completely, I'm aware of that. However, I adhere by the claim that the indictments against those men were drafted in such a way that their Defence counsel did not deal with the same problem as we are dealing with. I repeat, this is not correct. The HVO was -- the HVO was independent. There was no coordination, planning or organisation of any activities that I would be aware of, and it seems to me that I know everything. So there was nothing that would be conducted by the Croatian Army. Second of all, the units that we're talking about, especially Thunderbolts and Tigers that I personally requested, in military terms, they were much less significant than allowing us to say, Here we have volunteers. These brigades had a status and the combat readiness of the HVO was raised by 30 per cent when people who fought in Vukovar and in all the other battle-fields in Croatia arrived and joined them as volunteers. And then when Ms. Nika re-examines me, I will explain once again very precisely what the volunteers meant in a psychological sense, because in any case their numbers were not significant at all in military terms. Just in passing, let me say that there were other volunteers there, like Italians and other countries, just like there were volunteers from at least ten Islamic countries as Mujahedin, just like people from Russia and Greece fought on the side of the Serbs. That theory was non-defended, in procedural terms. It just went like that. Nobody defended it. I am defending it. We have documents. Let somebody show me at least one document proving that any of the actions were organised, planned, and coordinated in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, General, so let me take you to the next document which is closer to the front of the binder, 3D00909. It's one of your documents, 3D00909. It should be closer to the front.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, just again with reference to the previous document, P06037, which was the report to Brigadier Kapular on the report of the 5th Guards Brigade deployment in Herceg-Bosna, this is also a report now from Brigadier Kapular directed to Mr. Susak, the minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia, and this report is about the same subject; overview of the 5th Guards Brigade engagement in the territory of the Croatian Republic Herceg-Bosna. Now, and this was, as was indicated in the other report, 6037 that we looked at yesterday, Brigadier Kapular is reporting to Gojko Susak that: "On the 6th of July, 1993, a reinforced combat group was transferred from their combat activities in Zadar hinterland to the port of Ploce. As arrived, it was engaged in attack activities in the area of Mostar battle-field in order to defend the HR Herceg-Bosna efficiently and appropriately. As of 6th of July, 1993, to nowadays, the 5th Guards Brigade was entirely, in terms of its formation, engaged in Croatian Republic Herceg-Bosna in three shifts. Due to inability of HVO to organise for us the shift of manpower from its troops, we, by ourselves, had to secure the shift with our own units." Then he just talks -- in paragraph A he talks about the first shift, which is from a period 6th July to 28 July, which is just after you took command of the HVO Main Staff, General, and what he says is that: "One combat group, counting 360 men, was engaged on the Mostar battle-field," skipping a few words: "It was reinforced with squad cannon Howitzer, 155-millimetre D-20, three cannons, Howitzers." It says: "6th of July, 1993, parallel with the first shift, the brigade command directed 26 high-ranked officers to the HVO command in order to help the Main Staff of HVO to the command of rendezvous area of HVO and HVO brigade commands in order to make efficient war and to defend the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. One part, nine officers, are still involved in combat tasks in composition of the said commands on high levels." So, General, can you confirm for me, since you were present and since you took command of the HVO Main Staff on the 24th of July, that this is correct, that Brigadier Kapular's report to the Croatian defence minister about the deployment of these HV -- and I know that your position is that they're volunteers, but that these Croatian Army units, soldiers, and equipment were, in fact, deployed, as indicated here, not only in combat activities, but also high-ranking officers placed within and working within the Main Staff of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: One guards brigade, Mr. Stringer, does not have 26 high-ranking officers. A guards brigade can have maybe three or four high-ranking officers. None of those men were engaged in the Main Staff. I checked subsequently just to be able to tell you that even Kapular was not engaged in the Main Staff while I was there. I tried to remember, and I arrived at the number of maybe five or six men who were not high-ranking officers, but just officers, who were volunteers and wanted to assist some HVO brigades, so this is not correct. The brigade did not have 26 high-ranking officers, and they were certainly not engaged. And you can see that Mr. Kapular, who was in Vukovar, who was a formidable fighter, look at his calculation where he says: "Currently deployed units," and then he says --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me just follow up with a little bit. I understand that you're not accepting the assertion here by Brigadier Kapular that 26 high-ranking officers were placed within the HVO command. Something you just said, though, I want to come back to. You just said: "I checked subsequently just to be able to tell you that even Kapular was not engaged in the Main Staff while I was there." Now, General, yesterday we looked at P03957, which is in your binder, and you talked about it, and you talked -- and you told us about your request to the defence minister, Mr. Susak, that Brigadier Kapular be placed within the Main Staff for combat readiness. Do you remember that testimony yesterday? 3957 shows it. You asked for and you received Brigadier Kapular to come work as part of your Main Staff for combat readiness; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the way you describe it. I did not ask for him. He wanted to stay, and upon his approval to stay, I asked for the request. And this was the paper that was covering his death or wounding, but this was never approved. Although he wanted to come, obviously the 5th Guards Brigade needed him for some internal changes that were underway, so I did try to put him on the Main Staff. He did not become a member of the Main Staff. He certainly wasn't brought in. He hailed from Capljina, and he was in the area as a volunteer. But if you will allow me, now look at the sum --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, excuse me, I need to clarify. You just told us now he was in the area as a volunteer. Two minutes ago, you told us that he was in Vukovar, General, so let's just clear this one up first. Brigadier Kapular, the commander of the 5th Guards Brigade, which I think we agree had a substantial component of its units present in Herceg-Bosna during July, August, and September of 1993, was Kapular present down there during that period of time or was he not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now, first of all, Mr. Stringer, you tell us a story, you say he was in Vukovar, and then you ask me just one thing. I don't accept your stories. Mr. Kapular came from Canada, as a Canadian citizen of Croatian origins. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, you are escaping. You are going astray and avoiding to answer the question, which is a very, very simple "yes" or "no" question. Read it again and answer it, whether Kapular was present down there during that period of time or not. It's got nothing to do where he came from, from Canada, or Russia, or whatever, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, let me just -- I'll rephrase the question. This report and the one before it talks about units and equipment from the 5th Guards Brigade coming to Herceg-Bosna as from the 6th of July, 1993. Now, during the month of July 1993, to your knowledge, was Brigadier Kapular present in Herceg-Bosna and was he participating in the combat activities down there in a military or in a professional capacity? July 1993.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's just be very precise. We're not talking about July. 24th July is the time when I was commander. Please, not July, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me starting from my date, not the whole July but the 24th of July, when I became the commander. From then on, I can provide very precise answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, you don't get to ask the questions, then, that you're going to answer. I get to ask the questions. You were present in this region throughout July of 1993. We know that. And so as a person who was present down there, you're qualified to tell us, if you know, was Kapular down there in Herceg-Bosna fighting with or as a part of the HVO. Based on your personal knowledge, do you know; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, or you, Judges, you may get cross with me, but you cannot ask me a question starting with, You were in the area. A person cannot be in an area. I told you I was in Boksevica. I told you when I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Would you please just answer the question instead of arguing. You are not here to argue. You are in the role of a witness, under oath. You must say the truth. This is a simple question which you can answer by "yes" or "no," and it's not for you to discuss it and to tell anybody in the courtroom what kind of questions you should be asked. If something is wrong with a question, you have a Defence counsel who will intervene, and the Judges will intervene if something goes wrong, but you are not here to argue. You decided that you would be a witness, and here is a very, very simple question and you are to answer it, full stop. "Yes," "no," "I don't know," "I don't remember."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what you're saying is not correct. It's not a simple question that was put to me, no. I'm a witness testifying about the truth. You should answer, then. I wasn't in the area. I wasn't in the area. So there it is. It's very simple. I wasn't in the area, and as of the 24th of July I became the commander. And you're claiming that I was in the area. I wasn't there. I was in Boksevica as a soldier. You're expecting me to answer a question put to me that would lead me to give a false answer. What do you want me to do, Judge Trechsel? Do you want to depict me as an idiot? I'm not an idiot. You're an honourable Judge, but I'm not an idiot. I was in Boksevica, and I did not know what Kapular was doing until the 24th of July, 1993. That's a precise answer. And as of the 24th, he was occasionally in the area. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes, now it's okay. So, Mr. Praljak, you are not an idiot, but -- and nobody implies that, but it is really a question of fact. If you claim that you were not there and you do not know, then you have to answer that "I do not know," and that's over. I really don't understand why you're arguing on this very simple issue. Either you know the facts there or not. Then, in this case, you will say, "No, I was not there, I do not know," full stop. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I also have a comment to make, Mr. Praljak. Your behaviour here is not correct. You are showing disrespect to the Judges, you are arguing with me. That is not your role. I feel that you lack respect to the Judges, full stop. And please, Mr. Stringer, continue. No. While I have the floor, Mr. Stringer, could you give us a date for this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can. I can give you what I think is the date, because as you've indicated -- as you've noticed, the date -- the document doesn't bear a date. I would suggest, and the General and others maybe can disagree if they wish, it appears to me that P06037, which was the earlier report to Kapular from the subordinate, which is dated 23 October, then formed part of the basis for Brigadier Kapular's report which we're talking about now, because there's a lot of similarity in the information. And so based on that and the time-frames that are referred to in the Kapular report, 00909, it's our -- it's my belief or suggestion that the document is from late October 1993. But that takes some -- you have to read it in light of the earlier report and in light of the things that are being said, because the document, itself, does not have a date on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, the exchange that has just taken place, well, I'm responsible for this indirectly. Yesterday, when you discussed document P6037, you said at one point that Brigadier Kapular was in Zagreb. When you said that, I said to myself, well, this is strange. How is it that Kapular, who is supposed to be in Bosnia-Herzegovina, is in fact in Zagreb? At that time, I felt like putting the question to you and saying, Why are you saying that he is in Zagreb when we have every reason to believe that he is in Bosnia-Herzegovina? And I didn't put the question. Since I had already put a lot of questions, I felt I should stop. But had I put the question to you yesterday, this issue would have not arisen today. True to fact, the document dated the 23rd of October, 1993, the report is drafted by Dragan Boricic, is addressed to the Ministry of Defence in Zagreb and to Brigadier Kapular. Therefore, we know that on the 23rd of October, he is in Zagreb, since we have a document that states that. This is why we have a problem. Why is he there when, as Mr. Stringer indicated a few moments ago, you had asked him to come? I'm sure you have an answer to give us. I have understood that before the 24th of July, you were a soldier and you were saying that you didn't know. However, on the 24th of July, you said that Kapular came on two or three or four occasions, so I don't remember, but if in October he's back in Zagreb, this means that, in fact, he was not on a permanent basis in Bosnia and Herzegovina. You could have told this yesterday already, which would have avoided today's problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we'd have avoided all the problems if I were allowed to tell the truth without attempts being made to -- Mr. Kapular, from the 24th onwards, was, according to all the information I had, and I had information because he'd report to me, that on two, three, or four occasions, he visited the people there. The volunteers were down there. He was with them. Mr. Leko, rather, was with them. And Mazar, someone from Vukovar who'd died in the meantime, who destroyed 30 tanks in Vukovar. So there were people there. What I'm saying is that there weren't this many people, and I want to point out that under item -- he says 697 men. And, Judge Antonetti, you have your calculator. It's 563 men, and this report doesn't tally with the report from the field that we had a look at yesterday. I know why such doctored reports are produced, but no one asks me about that. And when I try to explain something, then it seems as if I fail to respect the Court, the Chamber. I do respect the Court, but I can't tell what is not true. To be a soldier in Boksevica is one thing, and, Judge Prandler, I can't say I wasn't there then, but I wasn't in the field. When you say in the field, you're trying to suggest that I know everything. Boksevica, in the field, means I'm a soldier, I stand guard and that I open fire in order to save 300 people in a certain area. These are very precise things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, how is it, then, that the 5th Guards Brigade, or part of it, is in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the commander of this, Kapular, is not there? Do you have any explanation for this or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can answer that, yes. These men are volunteers in the brigade. 80 per cent of the brigade in Croatia was performing its duties as the 5th Guards Brigade. They had to restructure. They had suffered losses, significant losses in Maslenica. This had to be dealt with -- I apologise, I do apologise. The brigade -- the 5th Guards Brigade is in Croatia at its positions. These men are volunteers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I should have perhaps put the question to you yesterday. The 5th Guards Brigade of the Republic of Croatia, well, what is its total strength?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The brigade had over 3.000 men, according to all my information, 3.000 and I don't know how many exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3.000. Fine. So out of this 3.000 men, if we understand this document before us properly, there would be approximately 600, but you said there were less than that. That would be one-fifth, so, i.e., 20 per cent. So 20 per cent of the men of the 5th Guards Brigade are volunteers in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at the same time. From the 24th -- well, when the second shift arrived on the 28th, I said that there were about 250 of them who arrived, perhaps a little more, and then this shift was replaced by another shift that had more or less the same number of men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, which would explain why, if the greatest number of men of the 5th Guards Brigade have their commander in Zagreb and not in Bosnia-Herzegovina, is that the answer you are giving us to the question why Kapular is there and not in this other country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. They had duties at the Zadar battle-field and around Vinkovci too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why didn't you say so? Why didn't you tell Mr. Stringer when he put the question to you? Had you said that straightaway, this -- we could have settled the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But when I'm asked a question, I provide a very simple answer, Judge Antonetti. But he says he was in Vukovar. How was it that he was there? You were in the field in that area, and then I don't know what the question is anymore. When a question is put to me throughout these proceedings, I've provided all the information I had in an honest manner. I've tried to present the truth in response to all the questions put to me. You don't agree with me, Judge Trechsel, but why are you shaking your head like that? Please, I do respect you, but, please, you shouldn't always have such an expression when I'm saying I'm telling the truth. Your facial expression says, Praljak, you're lying. That's what you are saying. It's not a matter of respecting the Court; it's a matter of what I can perceive in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to say that everything started with the question put by the Prosecution, which is on page 11 of the transcript, line 1. The question was: "You were in the area in July 1993, in the course of July 1993?" In response to that question, the General said: "You can put questions to me, but you can't ask me whether you were in that area. I told you that I was in Boksevica." So it's not true that the general did not answer the question, but the question was phrased in such a way that the answer couldn't have been different. The general didn't spend the entire month of July in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina or, rather, in the territory of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, this document starts with the period 6 July 1993. Is it your testimony that from the 6th of July, 1993, to the 24th of July, 1993, you do not know whether Brigadier Kapular was present in Herceg-Bosna, fighting with or working with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: After the 24th of July, then, which is when you take command of the HVO Main Staff -- P03957 is the document we looked at yesterday, which was your request to the Croatian Defence Ministry and Minister Susak to have Tole, Kapular, come down and work with you, if I can put it that way. And in your testimony yesterday on that I asked you -- this is page 43039 of the transcript: "Did Kapular come and take a position in the Main Staff of the HVO, as requested here?" And your answer: "For combat readiness. I don't know if anyone knows what that means, 'combat readiness.' The Main Staff -- or, rather, I had assistants for combat readiness, for the infantry and so on and so forth. Kapular was to assume some of those duties. He did assume certain duties. I don't know when Gojko Susak released him, I couldn't say so right now, but he released him. And he was born in a village near Capljina, and he assumed certain duties in the HVO Main Staff." And I asked you then, skipping down a couple lines: "Despite assuming these duties in the Main Staff for combat readiness, did Kapular at the same time keep his position as commander of the 5th Guards Brigade of the Croatian Army?" And your answer was: "It's quite certain that at the time he wasn't acting as the commander of the guard, so someone else was replacing him until he returned to the Croatian Army. So the position he previously had was frozen temporarily." So, General, from that and from what you're telling us today, can we conclude that as from the 24th of July or early August 1993, Brigadier Kapular came down and assumed duties within your Main Staff of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, when I answered that question I believe I remember that he was there. When I said "at home," I meant in detention. When I was in detention, I was wondering about whether Kapular was there or not. I thought he was when I answered your question. And then I couldn't remember, and I have the impression that he wasn't there. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So are you telling us that your testimony from tomorrow [sic] -- are you taking that back now? The testimony I just read to you from yesterday, you take that back, that's not right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say anything for certain, as I can't remember correctly. Much time has passed. The war was atrocious. So with all my goodwill -- well, at the time I was wondering about whether he was there or not. And I said if he was down there, then in that case he couldn't have been the commander, because you can't reconcile the two. But then when I returned in the evening, I tried to think about all the details, and now I can no longer remember whether he was there or not, whether he was released or not. So I really can't answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. General Praljak, the document which is quoted, 3957, which is a request which you sent to the Croatian government to have Kapular and Tole join you, this document is dated the 4th of August, which means that on the 4th of August, at any rate, he's not there, he's in Croatia, because you're asking him to join you. That's the first point. Second point. Kapular heads a brigade that comprises 3.000 men, which is, I'm sure, a well-known brigade and a respected and qualified brigade. What interest would he have to join the Herceg-Bosna HVO in -- to command which men? The mere fact that you asked him to come, well, first of all, did he agree to it or not, and did he come? This is what the question is all about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he agreed. I asked for him for combat readiness. He was an excellent combatant. I needed someone who would go from unit to unit to bolster the soldiers' morale, to assist. But now I'm no longer certain that he came, and now I have the impression that he didn't come. So I'm not certain about this. Because the war in Vakuf was terrible, I don't know -- there's no war here so that you can see how it is. There were hundreds of dead and wounded, and as a result it's impossible to remember all of this. Why did he want to come? Because he's from Herzegovina. He's from Bosnia and Herzegovina. He was, in fact, a volunteer in Croatia, as I was. He was born in Zvirovici. I know the village and the house that he was born in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, let's move to paragraph B of this document, 3D00909, which relates to the period of time when you were the commander of the HVO Main Staff. Kapular writes, and this is about the second shift -- and by the way, before I get to that, I want to go back to the top, based on something you said. You indicated that something less than the entire 5th Guards Brigade was deployed or present in Herceg-Bosna. I want to challenge you on that just a bit, because at the top, in the first paragraph, Brigadier Kapular writes that: "As from 6th of July, 1993, to nowadays, the 5th Guards Brigade was entirely, in terms of its formation, engaged in Herceg-Bosna in three shifts." So the fact is that when you consider that the 5th Guards Brigade went down to Herceg-Bosna in three shifts, when you consider all three shifts, then what the commander of this unit is saying is that, in fact, it turned out that the entire 5th Guards Brigade at one point or another went down to Herceg-Bosna and fought with the HVO; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Stringer. The report from the field that we examined yesterday is a lot more precise. I'll repeat what I said. Have a look at item C. It says "697." And when you add 563 to that, well, he doesn't even perform addition correctly, let alone do other things well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's put it this way, General: You're saying that the commander of the 5th Guards Brigade doesn't know or is incorrect when he's reporting to his minister of defence about the extent to which his unit, the 5th Guards Brigade, was deployed in Herceg-Bosna? You know better than him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know why he wrote this, and I know this better than he does because his men were with me and I was with them. And in a report that I drafted, I wrote down the 5th Guards Brigade, and 140 men were referred to. I practically knew each individual person, I knew how many of them there were. And here he's trying to attain certain objectives; glory for the brigade, he wants a little money as a benefit for battle-field duties, etc. He needs to get new cannons, so he says, here, the’ve been sent, but then he says some have broken down, and so on and so forth. So this is what is done in all organisations. Things are doctored, and things are doctored in the military, too, for very prosaic reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So your testimony, then, General, is this highly effective brigadier in the Croatian Army, who you've said nothing but good things about since we started talking about him, now your testimony is that he's making a false report about the deployment of his 5th Guards Brigade in Herceg-Bosna and that he's knowingly giving this false report to his minister of defence in order to get more equipment or more notoriety; is that your testimony? He's lying to Susak for improper reasons?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's doctored the report. That's done in all armies throughout the world, and especially at a time of war. 90 per cent of the reports are doctored, and I can't address this issue here because no one asks me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, the fact is, General, that if there was anyone who had a motive to lie about this issue, it's you; isn't that right? The fact is you're not telling us the truth fully about the deployment of the 5th Guards Brigade down in Herceg-Bosna, you're the one who's lying about this. Brigadier Kapular had no reason to lie, and in fact it would be counterproductive and risky, from a professional point of view, for him to lie to Minister Susak. He's got no reason to do that. You're the one who's got the motive to lie. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to ask my learned friend, Mr. Stringer, to refrain from expressing himself in that way. When Prosecution witnesses were present and when one of the Defence members told the witness that he was lying, then counsel was warned not to tell the witness that the witness was lying. So I would like to request that Mr. Stringer refrain from using such expressions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't mind. I'll answer the question, so long as I'm allowed to answer it. Why is it that I'm not lying, Mr. Stringer? In the report from the Uskoplje battle-field from this period of time, and I asked that the HVO -- the entire HVO should report on the actual state of men engaged. I don't know if you remember that document from 1993, and there I enumerated twenty one and mentioned who was ill and who wasn't there. It says the 5th Guards Brigade, 140, 50 men, so why would I then lie to myself, since I knew all these men? And, secondly, look, as I have said, under C it says the third shift is there, and what's the number? When he did the calculations, he wrote down "697."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. You're telling me I'm a liar. Allow me to defend myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, we're going to talk about the third shift, but I want to talk about the second shift first. So we'll get there, I promise you. The second shift, as indicated in item B, according to Brigadier Kapular, is from 28th of July until the 28th of September, 1993. This was the Second Combat Group consisting of approximately 700 men, engaged within combat activities on the Mostar and Uskoplje-Prozor battle-front. Isn't that true, General, that during this period of time you had some 700 men come down from the Croatian Army, with all of their equipment, to assist you in the conflict against the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct, not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. But Brigadier Kapular goes on to say -- he's talking about the first part of the combat group, some 310 men engaged in the Rama-Uskoplje battle-field on the 28th of July, 1993. Is that part correct, since this was right after you took command of the Main Staff on the 28th of July? Do you accept that Brigadier Kapular is saying here that 310 of his men were engaged on the Rama-Uskoplje battle-field, or is he not telling the truth to Minister Susak about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 245 men, according to Vinko Mazar's report, who is a commander from the 5th Guards Brigade. This is a document that you can look at, you showed it yesterday, 245 men, and the second group was not in Mostar. There may have been few men left behind, but there weren't -- in any case, 245 men in total, including drivers and -- and Mazar writes that in his correct report to his commander. And then, in turn, that one doctors the facts, adds up numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So when you say someone's doctoring the numbers, is this Brigadier Kapular you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Brigadier Kapular is the one who increased the figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, skipping down a couple of lines, but again staying with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Stringer. I have a question regarding this. Mr. Praljak, who was Major Z. Zeko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Leko, L, Leko. Zvonimir Leko. He was a Herzegovinian by origin. He fought in Vukovar. He was wounded three times. A formidable lad. He was the commander of that group or, rather, the infantry group of 140-plus men. He fought with them in Rama, and at one point he spent 40 days in a row in a trench until he was completely exhausted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you are testifying under oath. You are supposed to tell the whole truth. When you claim that the 5th Brigade was not there, you may be right about it, maybe it's not the truth. I have nothing to make any finding whatsoever. However, you know that the Prosecution has a lot of means available by September. For instance, they can launch investigations to trace back Kapular. I don't know whether he's still alive; to try and find Major Zeko; to try and find all those who were in the 5th Brigade, in the 5th Guards Brigade. And the Prosecution can, end of August, early September, come back with all those statements, saying that, Throughout that time, we all were in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, under Kapular's command. So, you see, technically it is feasible for them. And if the Prosecution decides to do so, what would you do then, what would you say? You, yourself, of course, with your investigators, can do the same thing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you give me additional time and if you tell me, Bring Mr. Leko, he's going to be here within 24 hours. Or if you say, Bring Mazar here, he will be here within 24 hours. Or ask me to bring here Brekalo, Juric, or any other. All of them will come within the next 24 hours. Just give me additional time and tell me who you want to see, which of the people you want to see here to tell you the truth, and they will be here. There you go. Okay, I can ask for additional investigation. I would like this to be checked either by the Trial Chamber, the Prosecutor, the Defence, whoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My fellow Judge wants to speak. But if I understand properly, you're telling me that all the members of the 5th Brigade, if they were to be heard, would confirm what you say; namely, that there were volunteers and that the 5th Brigade of the Republic of Croatia were not entirely, as is claimed by this document, there, but that some were there as volunteers. I just note what you say. But Judge Trechsel has a question, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just one information I would like to have about Major Leko. It's wrongly transcribed in the translation. Where did he hail from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Do you know the village or town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know where Leko hailed from, exactly which village. But for your information, Your Honour Judge Trechsel, he was an HVO member from the year 1992, when I came down there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. As far as you know, Ivan Kapular, just the same as Ante Roso, or Gotovina, or Milenko Filipovic, had they been soldiers in the French Foreign Legion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I believe that Kapular, and I say "I believe," that he was a member of the Canadian Army, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, this is what Kapular says about the first part of the combat group that went to Rama-Uskoplje on the 28th of July. He says, this is at the very bottom of the first page of the English: "If the first part of the combat group hadn't been used, the entire town of Uskoplje would have fallen." Would you agree with his assessment of that, in terms of the impact that the Croatian Army soldiers had in the balance of power, if you will, as between the HVO and the armija at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the hundredth time, they were not HV soldiers, they were HVO volunteers. I admire your persistence. You're going to ask me a hundred times, and I'm going to repeat a hundred times. They were volunteers in the HVO, and in military terms I was their commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they were -- let me answer. Yes, they meant a lot. They were formidable fighters, first-class fighters. They were very courageous, and they left in October, after having lost ten men, and they had over a hundred wounded, and all that after they had fought in Vukovar and Zadar. I believe that at the end of that stint as volunteers of the HVO, half of the brigade perished.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And it wasn't just these quality fighters who came down from the Croatian Army, it was also the big guns and the equipment, the MTS that they brought with them, that helped carry the day for the HVO on the Uskoplje-Rama battle-field; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, but not to the extent described here by Commander Kapular. The answer is yes, but not in the amount stated herein.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, we can talk about the third shift now, which he says is from the 28th of September, and he's saying that: "Currently located in Herceg-Bosna." He said that brigade units are currently engaged on lines, defence of the town of Uskoplje, and then he mentions Stublic and then in-depth Prozor. He gives a list of the currently deployed units, the 4th Motorised Battalion, one-third of the motorised battalion, a tank company. We can all read all of that. And then he concludes that the total number of engaged number of men on the field, 697. So, in fact, General, and I note this is one of your documents, which appears to have been made in the later part of October 1993, in fact, even as of that time, according to Brigadier Kapular, there was a very, very large contingent of the HV -- 5th Guards Brigade still present in Herceg-Bosna; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, do your sums and you will see it says "697." My sum is 563. The difference is 164. In the report, sent on the 18th of September from the same theatre of war by Commander Vinko Mazar, says we have a total of 245 men. And I'm telling you, these are war reports that contain errors in all wars, in all armies. It's up to you whether you want to believe me or not. Maybe you can consult some books on war doctrine. Every commander will say that they have less ammunition than they actually do. Everybody who's in charge of an ammunition depot says that they have less than they should. People are requesting more than they actually need. It's only natural. But let me not go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 2, he says that: "From the 6th of July until now, within the combat activities on the battle-fields of HR Herceg-Bosnia, save the manpower of the brigade, the following combat technique was engaged:" I'm not sure how good that translation is. He makes reference to eight tanks, eight T-55s, and you'll recall perhaps, General, that that number is the one that's also contained in the exhibit we looked at yesterday, P06037. And if you keep that number in mind, eight tanks, if you skip down to item 4, he's talking about what the brigade -- the assets of the brigade in total, and he indicates that the brigade has 25 T-55 tanks. So that would suggest, wouldn't it, General, that about one-third of the brigade's tanks, 8 of the 25 of them, were actually deployed down in Herceg-Bosna as part of the combat activities there against the Armija of Bosnia-Herzegovina, is that correct, eight T-55 tanks?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not while I was there, there were not eight tanks there. In the battle-field where they were deployed, and that was Vakuf, there were three tanks. I believe that there was an RAK. And I really can't remember that they brought a 152-millimetre Howitzer D-20. While I was in command, this fact does not stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So your recollection is that there were three tanks of the Croatian Army that were in the area of Gornji Vakuf during this period, which is roughly August-September 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct that there were three Croatian Army tanks. Three tanks came from Croatia and became the tanks of the HVO, and at the end of the day, when it came to the hierarchy, I was in command of those tanks. They were not HV tanks; they were HVO tanks. Now, as for the origin of things that came to Bosnia and Herzegovina, if we were to count the states involved, then half of the world would be involved in that war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's where they all came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit that I have here is P06468. This is dated the 6th of November, 1993, and these are appointments made by Mr. Gojko Susak and Janko Bobetko, who is the chief of the Main Staff of the Croatian Army. And they are appointing various individuals to the Main Staff of the HVO. Do you see this? Do you have the document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, were you familiar with this fact? This is just at the time that you are resigning your position as commander of the HVO Main Staff. Were you aware, General, that pursuant to an order of the supreme commander of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia, President Tudjman, that these 14 individuals are being appointed by General Bobetko and by Gojko Susak, first among those being Ante Roso, who, in fact, took command of the HVO Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of those problems. Franjo Tudjman, the commander of the HV, never issued an order for something to that effect to be written. He never signed anything of that kind, either him or Susak or Bobetko. I know that there was a huge misunderstanding with this regard and that this was actually done by somebody who tries to be very smart. This document does not have a signature. It's not valid. Franjo Tudjman was very cross when he saw this, and he said, What kind of a moron is able to write something like this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And President Tudjman was so cross because he was worried that if this document or something like this were to fall into the hands of, for example, some of the European countries or the Americans, that it could result in severe repercussions for the Republic of Croatia; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Tudjman was worried, thinking, Who is it who could write something like that, for him to order another army to appoint people to the Main Staff. He can release volunteers, he can promise them promotion, but Mr. Tudjman was too clever a gentleman to appoint army commanders in a different state. He was not so much concerned about America, and so on and so forth, although he had to bear that in mind as well. He knew very well that such a nonsense could shed a totally wrong light on what was going on in Bosnia and Herzegovina, especially among those who managed the war and were making it take the directions that it did, and there were a lot of such people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But isn't it true, General, that in fact it was President Tudjman who did ultimately make the appointments and the decisions, albeit perhaps not officially or formally, but it was President Tudjman who appointed and approved persons such as you, Milivoj Petkovic, Ante Roso, Lasic, Siljeg? All of you from the Croatian Army, in fact, would not have held the positions you held in the HVO if President Tudjman did not approve of that? Isn't that how it really was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Was it your testimony that it was Mate Boban who had the ultimate authority on the appointments to the command positions in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Mate Boban could appoint and dismiss or discharge. He could talk to anybody he wanted to, he could take advice, but he was the one who appointed people. And he appointed me because he needed me, because I had the knowledge, I had a high -- which you also checked during your investigation, I had a reputation among lads, and he needed me. And I, myself, wanted to fight after having spent a year on peacemaking. But, please, do not forget one thing. I am a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So it's your testimony, General, that President Tudjman played no role in the appointment of officers to command positions in the HVO; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my testimony. A role is one thing; an appointment is a different thing. You can play a role as an adviser. You can assist with something being done. You can help, you can raise the level of motivation in order to help people make a decision to go somewhere, but all that does not fall under the category of decision. Decision was not Franjo Tudjman's. Franjo Tudjman could arm the BiH Army. He negotiated with Alija Izetbegovic, who in turn negotiated with the international community. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mate Boban was the one who appointed commanders and discharged them of their duties; up to the brigade level, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit is P06797. This a document of the Republic of Croatia Ministry of Defence, Welfare Administration, 22 November 1993. Just one last little bit about the southern front, General. The person who's writing this order, Mr. Blaskovic, Boris Blaskovic, he's sending this out to the operations zones and the heads of the welfare departments and the Operative Administration of the Defence Ministry, and he says: "This is an order to be very careful during filling out of death forms so that in the case of a person killed in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, one is supposed to fill in the southern battle-field and not the exact place of death. The matter is that this has been still happening, especially in the recent time, that some people are mentioning the name of the place of death as, for example, Mostar, Bugojno or other places." Now, is it true, General, that the Croatian public, the families of those who died in Bosnia-Herzegovina, would have been misled about the place of death and that this was, in fact, a cover-up to prevent the world from knowing that you had a lot of soldiers from the Croatian Army who were fighting and dying on the battle-field in such places as Bugojno and Mostar in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single Croatian soldier was killed. They were killed as HVO members. And why is this gentleman writing this? He's writing this precisely for the fact that I've already repeated several times. Peace will come. There will be bureaucrats, there will be red tape, and if they died as HV volunteers, somebody will say, You are not entitled to a pension or your families are not entitled to pension, or you're not entitled to treatment. The fact that they had to be mentioned as having been killed in the southern front is a social problem, not a psychological problem. People who went down there were volunteers, as professionals. And as for what the general public thinks about war is important, but not as important as defending a people from the brutal aggression launched by an army that were allies until only yesterday, and that at the moment when the international community established a republic and when Alija Izetbegovic wanted to extend his own republic all the way down to the sea.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, the fact is, General, that this issue could have very easily been dealt with administratively and honestly and openly if the Croatian Ministry of Defence didn't want to cover up the fact that so many of its soldiers, on its payroll, entitled to pensions of the Croatian Army, were, in fact, engaging in and being killed in operations down in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This could easily have been dealt with without this sort of deceit; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this could not have been done in any other way. There's still a huge problem in Bosnia-Herzegovina, because members of the HVO are asking for their pensions that they received in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which are very low, to be equal to the pensions of the Croatian soldiers, because they believe, as everybody else does, that the Croats did not attack anybody; they only defended themselves. Both in Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the tension still persists. And after the war, Croatia made a number of donations to Bosnia-Herzegovina, which couldn't do it itself, to pay the HVO soldiers, their treatment, their pensions, their salaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer, I'm sorry to interrupt you. Concerning this order, in paragraph 3 we can read that: "All required forms are to be filled out correctly and completely; i.e., not only the information concerning the HV member," "concerning the HV member who had been killed, but also the information regarding his family members," et cetera. My question, Mr. Praljak, is: If, as you claim, if everybody -- there was a volunteer only and everybody who was killed, let's say quote/unquote "in the southern front," then why this order, in its paragraph 3, uses the expression "HV member"? It is my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if they say the HVO, then someone will say, The HVO, well, it's a different state, you can't do that. So as in the case of the Muslims, an HVO member, who voluntarily became an HVO member, but had his rights maintained, well, that was never in dispute. We arranged things so that they would maintain their rights, that the family of these men would have their rights, that he would -- so that he would be buried, so that he would be medically treated, as if he was a member of the HVO. Wherever he was killed, if he was a volunteer, he would be treated as if he were a member of the HVO. And that was the case in the ABiH as well, if you had a look at the documents, so when he goes there, his rank is waiting for him, his flat, his salary. So this was an overall position that has quite clearly been presented here. Someone will mistake -- confuse the HV and the HVO, but this position is absolutely clear wherever they went to fight against a common enemy. Well, if you left the HVO [as interpreted], wherever you went, you would have all the rights you would have had if you'd remained in the HVO [as interpreted]. That's what I've repeated, that's how it was, and I worked on this when I was the head in the IPD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, but I was not convinced. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. Stringer. For the sake of the transcript, the General, on page 36, line 8 to 10, spoke about the HV, not the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, for interrupting. I have been looking at the order, and I think it would be correct for me to say something. I can't see, in item 1 of this order, anything that has to do with the other items, and although Mr. Praljak is testifying here, I think we have to be cautious. These are instructions that are being given for all HV soldiers and their family members who have certain needs, so I don't see how items 2, 3 and 4 -- I don't see how these items have anything to do with item 1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, to be clear, this military document dates back to November. You were no longer holding the post then, so you could say that this document does not concern you, since you were no longer in any position of responsibility at the time. But let's set this aside. This document seems to show that there is a problem. When a soldier is killed in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, one should not mention the place of death, such as Mostar, Bugojno, or other places. Remember paragraph 195 of the Naletilic judgement. This Trial Chamber has made judicial notice of paragraph 195, which I'm going to read out slowly. I quote: "If voluntary defenders may have represented part of the Croatian troops present in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is in fact Croatia that organised the dispatch of the vast majority of them, while trying to hide or conceal their presence by asking them, for instance, to change uniforms and insignia, and by putting on HVO uniforms and insignia." End of quotation; Naletilic judgement, paragraph 195. So the Naletilic Trial Chamber had made the finding that the Republic of Croatia had concealed something. Now, we have this document here, and it may fall into this category of concealment, as it were. What do you say to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if the Republic of Croatia had tried to conceal something, such a document would never have been drafted, nor would there have been the initial documents from 1992. General Tus, myself, Gojko Susak's announcement, this was all public, and instructions were provided very precisely. They wouldn't have concealed Muslim documents where they said, Please release those people, they'll go to such and such places, but they'll retain the rights of the HVO or, rather, the HV. I apologise. I'm sorry I can't convince Judge Prandler, but it's simple. I worked on this as assistant minister for IPD. A volunteer who fights against a common enemy or who is defending the Croatian people has to take off his insignia when he goes to another army, to the HVO, he's under the command of the HVO, but if he's killed and while he's in that area, or if he is wounded, he'll be treated as if he were an HV soldier. He'll be receiving his salary, he'll be provided with medical care and hospital, because there were no hospitals down there. His family -- well, he'll be buried, he'll receive an allowance. I don't know what I could say about this. Nothing was concealed. These were volunteers, and I'm repeating what I said, at one point in time while I was down there during the most intensive fighting. As for the 24th of July until the 9th of November, there was never at any point in time more than 500 men down there, altogether. I also mentioned the figure of 700 with reference to Naletilic, and then I made certain calculations and I said 500, but at no point in time were there more than 500 volunteers, but 60 men from the Tigers, from the 1st Guards Brigade, meant a lot to me. They just rose up. It's as if a marine were to arrive on the scene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's time for the break. It is five minutes to 4.00, and we've over-stepped the time. We shall have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, I believe you have a correction to make on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, good day. Good day to everyone in the courtroom. As you requested, if we notice that there's some problems with the translated documents, we inform you at the time. I'd like to draw your attention to a problem that concerns the translation of document 3D909, which is a document that we spent the entire first session discussing. In the English text, the translation indicates that it concerns the entire 5th Guards Brigade that was engaged in Herceg-Bosna. That's literally stated in the fifth line of the English translation. The Croatian original, however, is different. In that part of the text, the Croatian original states that the 5th Guards Brigade, and I quote -- that "its entire establishment was engaged in Herceg-Bosna." I quote -- I repeat "it's entire establishment part" or, rather, "element was engaged in Herceg-Bosna." So reference is made to an establishment part of the 5th Brigade that was engaged in Herceg-Bosna. And if this is compared with the beginning of the passage, which refers to reinforced combat group, which in the -- from the hinterland of Zadar was transferred to Herceg-Bosna, and then it also refers to combat groups in the first and second shift, if this is done, I think it's clear that the 5th Brigade -- or, rather, the entire 5th Brigade wasn't engaged in Herceg-Bosna, as translated in the English version. So given the discussion with General Praljak, I was of the opinion that it was important to clarify this. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Alaburic, for having clarified this. To tell you the truth, I had a question about this. When I saw that in the English, words had been placed in brackets, I then looked at the B/C/S version. Since I'm not conversant in the B/C/S, I wondered whether this had been translated properly, and I had thought that the Defence counsel, who speak both languages, were going to make a comment. Notwithstanding that, I also did have a technical question that came to mind. When a unit or a brigade, i.e., 3.000 men, move from one place to another, this is an extremely sophisticated and complicated operation. Technically speaking, moving such a unit is always difficult. Part of the unit always remains in the barracks, there are maintenance vehicles, and not everybody goes from A to B, not all the people. So the adjective "entirely" did not fit in with the military situation in question. I was waiting for the B/C/S experts to say something about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Alaburic, for having pointed out a problem with translation. I would like to know what that means. I must say that the words that I have heard in English, I cannot make heads or tails of. I have no idea, whatsoever, what it is supposed to mean. So I don't know whether you can explain. Maybe I will listen to the French translation once more and then understand something. So far, I do not know what this means.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, I've spoken to General Petkovic as well, and we both tried to understand the meaning of this term, and we will now tell you what we believe it means. One brigade has its own establishment. It's a list of all the parts of the brigade or its components, and it includes all the positions, the duties in the brigade. There is something that is called an establishment part within a brigade, so that is something that comes under the description of all the organisational units and their tasks, so it's part of this organisation. And according to our understanding, in Herceg-Bosna a part of the brigade was engaged, and this depended on the volunteers who volunteered, and then such a part could be formed. If we then have a look at the first shifts and how men and equipment were engaged, we can see, in fact, what this part represented, this part of the 5th Guards Brigade. And according to our rough assessment, an assessment we made during the break, that would correspond to what General Praljak, in fact, said with regard to the total number of men in the territory of Herceg-Bosna as volunteers. And if we compare all the equipment that the 5th Guards Brigade had at its disposal with the equipment that was engaged in Herceg-Bosna, in that case this would also correspond to the assessment that was about -- it represented about one-third of the tanks, and so on and so forth. So this is how we understand this, but we admit that this expression is very unclear, but we believe that it can be interpreted within the relevant context as we have interpreted it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I have noted that what I have heard now was quite different from what you had first given, and you admit, yourself, that this is not clear. And, indeed, the method of interpretation that I understand and that I see here, is it is so interpreted by Mr. Praljak that it is corresponding to what he has said, this is natural, but it's, of course, far from objective and cannot be taken at face value. I think we'll have to -- we'll have to wait and hope that we get clarification on this. Of course, we are also interested to know what the effective number of military men in this 5th Guard Brigade are, because so far we have just one figure that has been given to us without any objective clarification. So all I can state is that this is something which is unclear. And you have helped, Ms. Alaburic, to point out the unclarity, which is of value, and I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, in view of the obvious importance, I think, that all the parties and the Trial Chamber attach to this document, which is one of the Praljak Defence documents, I mean, clearly we see, you know, translations -- this is an unofficial office translation. Prosecution translations have mistakes in them or sometimes can be improved upon. Perhaps this one can be improved upon as well. I don't know. I'm at a disadvantage to really comment on anything that counsel has said. Could I suggest, however, that perhaps we, one of the parties or even the Trial Chamber could ask the CLSS, who are really sort of the professionals at the highest level, to review the translation. Perhaps a revised or an approved CLSS version could be made that could be substituted for this if there's any significant difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is what we shall do. General Praljak, had you been more careful, you would have realised there was a problem. When the Prosecutor said that the 5th Guards Brigade was entirely in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you should have responded that, technically speaking, this was impossible. All you needed have done was to indicate, for instance, take the case of the US troops in Afghanistan. When one unit goes off to Afghanistan, there's always a group of men that remain behind in the USA. The same applies to France. This is a standard practice in the military. In this case, you didn't say anything, so one had -- one could have believed that you disagreed with the Prosecutor. And this adverb "entirely" did oppose the problem. You should have, with the technical expertise you have, stepped in and said something. It's not for me to correct this afterwards.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Antonetti. I quite simply wasn't paying attention to this. In 1993, I drafted a report in the course of the war. I would have been happy if there had been several thousand of them, but I wrote down a number in that document at the time, the document you've seen. In desperation, it says "Fuck it," if you remember those words. I then stated how many members of the 5th Guards Brigade were in Uskoplje. But in 1993, in such conditions, would I have lied, I would have been happy to have thousands of soldiers. Our situation was desperate, and the number is mentioned there. I know how many of them were there. I was in the war, and that's why I miss certain things like this. I understand that they are important to you. And I'm claiming that at the very same time in Zagreb, the ABiH received more from Croatia than the HVO. This included logistics bases, and thousands of Muslims were equipped in Croatia and sent to the ABiH. I don't understand this problem, I'm stupid in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, had you used your mental calculator, you would have realised when the Prosecutor gave us a breakdown of the units, the first, the second and the third, A, B and C of the documents, when you did the sum total of the figures that had been mentioned, we reached the figure of 2.000, approximately. And you said that the brigade comprised 3.000 men, so a thousand were missing, and you didn't notice that. Admittedly, when one answers questions for months and months, perhaps one is not so alert anymore. Fortunately, the Judges of the Bench are still able to do their sums.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I indicated the place where a mistake was made with regard to 150 men. The figure was increased by 150. I noticed that these figures are not correct. I know why they're not correct. I understand the brigade commander, who's fighting to obtain more. In Croatia, there was nothing. If you saw the document where it says there, No trousers, no boots, that's what it says. They had nothing, and he's struggling to obtain these things. So naturally, he will doctor the figures, and then he asks for these details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, the Trial Chamber will ask CLSS to translate this part of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, we're just about done with this set. One of the documents we looked at a few minutes ago was P06468, which was the document whereby there was an indication that pursuant to an order of President Tudjman, and on the, I guess, approval or the support of Gojko Susak and Janko Bobetko, a group of individuals from the Croatian Army were appointed to the HVO Main Staff, and the first among those being Ante Roso. Do you have 6468 there, or do you recall that one? And I know you challenged the document or you challenged whether President Tudjman was, in fact, making the appointment -- the appointments that are indicated here. Do you remember the document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If you'll just keep that in mind, because I want to move to the next one, which is P06831, which is one of the Presidential transcripts. It's from the 23rd of November, 1993. Now, General, I know that this is a meeting that takes place after you've resigned or given up your position in the HVO, but it relates to events that were taking place while you were with the HVO and while you were still associated with President Tudjman's government as an adviser. So I want to ask you some questions about it. It is on the 23rd of November, 1993. President Tudjman is there with Janko Bobetko and Gojko Susak. And I'd like to direct you to page 8 of the transcript, and I'm going to read some passages to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. President, just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you start, at the time I wasn't President Tudjman's adviser, so you shouldn't refer to facts that you haven't checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, I actually meant to say that I understand that you were not his adviser at the time. Maybe that wasn't interpreted correctly.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So just for reference, Mr. President, on page 7, you'll see this is the transcript where President Tudjman asks who ordered the bridge in Mostar to be destroyed, and then turning to page 8, actually, they move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And that's the one I would like to talk to you about, General. The top of page 8, President Tudjman, after asking for a written report about the destruction of the Old Bridge, he says, and I'm quoting: "Thirdly, how, Minister of Defence and chief of the main headquarters, could you have issued such an order confirming that Croatia is waging war, that it is directly involved, and I constantly emphasise that you should have built all this up as something voluntary, that these are volunteers who have left the Croatian Army, who fight there under HVO command, and here you are appointing the main headquarters, minister of defence of Croatia and chief of the main headquarters." Now, we can go on, General Praljak, just to make it clear that what President Tudjman is referring to here is P06468, which was the document on the appointments to the HVO Main Staff. On the next page, President Tudjman says: "But not that we should make appointments --" Let me just back up a little bit. Bobetko says: "We here agreed that after the meeting here we should get together people who should help to work there." President Tudjman says: "But not that we should make appointments. It was said, if you please, that I released with my own order that stayed here, General Roso, but General Roso was appointed by the president of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna." And then skipping down a few lines, Bobetko says --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is -- are people having trouble following --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not being correctly interpreted. We'll go too far and I'll have to go back to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Mr. Stringer, you're being incorrectly interpreted into Croatian, so perhaps you should repeat what you said. There's a mistake that has been made, and it's quite important.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay, I'll start over. Thanks for the warning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me start with just the first quote that I read, where President Tudjman says: "Thirdly," now, "Thirdly," quote: "How, minister of defence and chief of the main headquarters, could you have issued such an order confirming that Croatia is waging war, that it is directly involved, and I constantly emphasise that you should have built all this up as something voluntary, that these are volunteers who have left the Croatian Army, who fight there under HVO command, and here you are appointing the main headquarters." Just to stay with that one, General, doesn't this essentially confirm that this whole business of volunteers was a sham and that essentially your testimony about these Croatian Army soldiers being volunteers is just a repeat of the sham that President Tudjman was talking about all the way back in November of 1993 as a way to mislead the international community and the world about Croatia's involvement in Herceg-Bosna?
